title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable,Navigable, and Editable
event_hint: Harness Handbook + BGPD: a behavior-centric handbook for agent harnesses improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality with fewer planner tokens.
problem: Behavior localization is a central bottleneck in evolving production agent harnesses: a modification request describes what behavior should change, but the repository is organized by files/functions/modules, while a single behavior is distributed across many nonadjacent sites spanning execution stages and shared state. Existing code search, repository maps, summarization, and long-context editing make code easier to inspect but still leave developers/agents to recover the behavior-to-code mapping by hand, and agents with limited context may overlook scattered or rarely executed paths.
mechanism: Harness Handbook is a behavior-centric representation built automatically in three phases (Algorithm 2, Appendix A): Phase I deterministic static fact extraction (language adapters parse functions, boundaries, signatures, call edges; unresolved calls are written to an audit log rather than assigned guessed targets; no LLM calls); Phase II behavioral organization maps source units onto an execution-stage skeleton using either function-as-leaf (starts from a trusted seed skeleton S0; budgeted stage and membership review, then region/ordering finalization) or file-as-leaf (describes files first and infers the skeleton; optional refinement) modes; Phase III hierarchical synthesis produces an L1-L3 document tree plus cross-stage state registers, with each entry linked to a statically identified source location. Phase III validates every L3 locator against the current repository and freezes entries that cannot be revalidated (excluding them from localization until refreshed), keeping the repository authoritative for implementation details. The packaged handbook retains a machine-readable synchronization state K_g (program graph, stage skeleton, mode-specific organization state, construction config Theta including organization/generation/register-extraction budgets, and generation cache; seed skeleton S0 retained only in function mode). Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD) guides agents from high-level behaviors down to implementation details and verifies candidate locations against current source; an automatic resynchronization step updates the handbook on repository change, limiting model calls to four semantic steps (classification, file assignment, within-stage organization, description revision).

evidence.claim: Handbook-Assisted planning raises overall win rates vs Baseline by 10.0 percentage points on Codex and 18.9 points on Terminus-2.
evidence.condition: 30 modification requests per harness; two harnesses (Codex Rust file-as-leaf, Terminus-2 Python function-as-leaf); Handbook-Assisted BGPD vs Baseline arms

evidence.claim: Planner token use falls by 12.7% on Codex and 8.6% on Terminus-2 with handbook assistance.
evidence.condition: Same planning tasks on the two evaluated harnesses

evidence.claim: With handbook guidance a weaker planner matches stronger reference models on Terminus-2: file-level F1 84.7% and 89.3%, symbol-level F1 77.1% and 89.3% against Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 references; precision reaches 93.3% against GPT-5.5 at both granularities.
evidence.value: File F1 84.7/89.3, symbol F1 77.1/89.3; precision 93.3% vs GPT-5.5
evidence.condition: Terminus-2; weaker planner + handbook; all 24 file/symbol Recall/Precision/F1 comparisons improved against two independent references
evidence.source_locator: Section 4.2 and Section 5 Conclusion, PDF Page 10

evidence.claim: Complete localization failures (Wrong = zero overlap vs reference) never increase with the handbook and fall by as much as 25.9 points.
evidence.value: up to 25.9 points reduction in Wrong rate

evidence.claim: All six harness-by-type win-rate comparisons favor the Handbook-Assisted arm, with gains of 16.3 to 33.3 percentage points; cross-file requests improve 16.3 and 20.0 points; Codex gains most on Query requests (+26.7) and Terminus-2 most on Search-Hostile requests (+33.3).
evidence.condition: Stratified by request type and localization difficulty across the two harnesses

evaluation_context: Two open-source agent harnesses differing by roughly two orders of magnitude: Terminus-2 (Python terminal agent from the Harbor framework, observe-decide-act loop over tmux; 6 source files, 103 internal-function nodes, 41 boundary nodes, 257 resolved call edges; function-as-leaf; built handbook has 20 L2 stages, 106 L3 entries, 10 state registers) and Codex (Rust monorepo behind the Codex coding agent; 2,267 files, 34,363 internal-function nodes, 4,016 boundary nodes, 159,960 resolved call edges; file-as-leaf; 140 L2 stages, 2,267 L3 entries, 62 state registers). 30 modification requests per harness balanced across request type and localization difficulty; two arms (Baseline vs Handbook-Assisted BGPD) with every factor other than handbook access held fixed; reference localization plans from Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5. Construction (Appendix A): Phase I is fully deterministic with no LLM; Phase II and Phase III are budgeted (organization/generation/register-extraction budgets recorded in config Theta) but the actual construction token/time cost and a net build-plus-resync cost-benefit are not reported.
limitations: Validated on only two harnesses (though they differ sharply in scale and language). Static analysis is conservative: unresolved calls are logged rather than assigned guessed targets, and content that cannot be parsed/classified is frozen or recorded in the coverage record; Phase III freezes any L3 locator that cannot be revalidated against the current repository. The specific weaker planner model whose F1/precision are reported is still not named in the visible evidence. The initial Handbook construction cost (Phase I-III) in tokens/model calls/time and a net build-plus-resynchronization cost-benefit are not quantified; only the qualitative fact that Phase I uses no LLM and that Phase II/III run under recorded budgets is available. Gain variation is not fully explained by labeled difficulty. The paper reports planning/localization quality and planner-token cost, not end-to-end executed task success rate or wall-clock latency.
project_relevance: Directly addresses the Agent语义加速 question of cutting repeated Read/Grep/context localization: a behavior-centric index lets an agent navigate from a requested behavior to source sites instead of iteratively exploring files, and it reports exactly the metrics the topic values (planner-token reduction of 12.7%/8.6% and localization F1/Precision). Caveat for project inference: it measures edit-plan/localization quality, not end-to-end task latency or success rate, and build/resync cost is only partly quantified (Phase I is LLM-free but Phase II/III budgets and totals are not reported); net benefit and applicability to general (non-harness) code search still need confirmation.

What is the initial Handbook construction cost (Phase I-III) in tokens/model calls/time, and does the paper report a net cost-benefit including build plus resynchronization?
